hero.headline: Port St. Lucie faces renewed flood threat with 4 to 6 inches of rain forecast
hero.teaser: Another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days in Port St. Lucie, threatening renewed flooding in neighborhoods still recovering from record rainfall two weeks ago
hero.body:
Another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days in Port St. Lucie, threatening renewed flooding in neighborhoods still recovering from record rainfall two weeks ago. St. Lucie Public Schools announced a two-hour early release Tuesday.

 County crews have been inspecting canals and drainage systems, clearing them ahead of the expected rain. Officials warn that the ground remains saturated from recent storms, meaning far less rain than usual could cause flooding in neighborhoods, streets and other low-lying areas. The school district announced the early dismissal to avoid a repeat of the flooding problems that affected students taking buses home earlier this month.

 The earlier flooding stranded cars, trapped some families in their homes and forced others to wade through deep water. “It was horrible,” said Port St. Lucie resident Crisostomo Santiago Perez. “Water was on top of the cars almost, covering hoods.” With more heavy rain forecast, Perez said he planned to get supplies before flooding returned.

 Freshman Noah Julian was among those caught in the earlier flooding. He stepped off his school bus to find his neighborhood along Coleman Avenue flooded. A video recorded by neighbor Martina Elieson spread quickly on social media, showing him swimming through floodwaters to reach his driveway. His father, Romeo Julian, expressed concern about alligators, snakes and sharp objects in the water.

 Residents are encouraged to monitor local forecasts and prepare for changing conditions as the rain moves into the area.

cards.headline: Martin County sheriff warns of e-bike seizures, possible charges against parents
cards.teaser: The Martin County sheriff warned Monday that deputies could seize illegal e-bikes and pursue criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. The w
cards.body:
The Martin County sheriff warned Monday that deputies could seize illegal e-bikes and pursue criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. The warning followed a Sunday crash near U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road that left a 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy with catastrophic injuries. The boy was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center and was in stable condition, the sheriff said at a news conference.

 The boy and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes when they attempted to cross U.S. 1, according to the sheriff. The friend made it across, but a northbound vehicle with a green light struck the 14-year-old. The impact threw the boy approximately 50 feet, and his e-bike landed about 100 feet away. The boy was wearing a helmet, which the sheriff credited with helping him survive the crash.

 Investigators determined that the boy was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The sheriff described the motorbike-style vehicle as illegal for street use. He said deputies are considering tougher consequences for illegal e-bike use, including seizures and possible criminal charges against parents who knowingly permit their children to ride the bikes.

 The sheriff reported 41 e-bike crashes in Martin County this year, involving riders ranging in age from 7 to 80. He said educational workshops, warnings and previous enforcement efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the investigation into Sunday's crash, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

cards.headline: Family Night set for Nov. 17 at Jensen Beach’s Festival of Giving
cards.teaser: Family Night will take place Tuesday evening, Nov. 17, at the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast in Jensen Beach during the third annual Festival of Giving. More than 50 local
cards.body:
Family Night will take place Tuesday evening, Nov. 17, at the Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast in Jensen Beach during the third annual Festival of Giving. More than 50 local nonprofit organizations are participating in the festival, which fills the museum with decorated Christmas trees and other holiday displays. The event combines seasonal decorations with an opportunity for visitors to learn about the organizations and the work they do across the region. Family Night is one of the activities scheduled during the festival, which also includes a Friday party for adults and continues through Saturday, Nov. 21.

 The participating nonprofits represent communities from Palm Beach County north through the Treasure Coast, according to Christina McIntosh, the museum’s community outreach and events coordinator. That geographic reach also connects with the museum’s educational work. “Those are the five counties that our education department here at the museum works with and works with the schools,” McIntosh said.

 The festival gives organizations serving South Florida and the Treasure Coast a place to introduce their missions to museum visitors. Its Christmas trees and holiday displays serve as a way to bring attention to the nonprofits and explain their work in the communities they serve.

 For participating organizations, the festival offers another benefit: a chance to become more familiar with other nonprofits in the region. Treasure Coast Community Singers is among the groups taking part in this year’s gathering. “The really great thing about this event is that we get to know other nonprofits,” said Sharon Savageaux of Treasure Coast Community Singers. “We get to understand what they do.” Alongside the public displays, that opportunity to learn about one another is part of the event’s purpose. The gathering brings more than 50 organizations into the same museum for a festival focused on both holiday decorations and community work.

 Later in the week, the celebration will shift to an adult holiday pajama party on Friday. “We will be a museum full of adults dressed in their holiday pajamas because who doesn’t want to go to a party and go home and go right to bed,” McIntosh said. The Friday event follows Tuesday’s Family Night as the festival moves toward its final day. According to McIntosh, the Festival of Giving continues through 2 p.m.

 Saturday, Nov. 21. The Children’s Museum of the Treasure Coast is at 1707 NE Indian River Drive in Jensen Beach. More information is available at www.childrensmuseumtc.org.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie faces renewed flood threat with 4 to 6 inches of rain forecast
hero.teaser: Another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days in Port St. Lucie, threatening renewed flooding in neighborhoods still recovering from record rainfall two weeks ago
hero.body:
Another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days in Port St. Lucie, threatening renewed flooding in neighborhoods still recovering from record rainfall two weeks ago. St. Lucie Public Schools announced a two-hour early release Tuesday.

 County crews have been inspecting canals and drainage systems, clearing them ahead of the expected rain. Officials warn that the ground remains saturated from recent storms, meaning far less rain than usual could cause flooding in neighborhoods, streets and other low-lying areas. The school district announced the early dismissal to avoid a repeat of the flooding problems that affected students taking buses home earlier this month.

 The earlier flooding stranded cars, trapped some families in their homes and forced others to wade through deep water. “It was horrible,” said Port St. Lucie resident Crisostomo Santiago Perez. “Water was on top of the cars almost, covering hoods.” With more heavy rain forecast, Perez said he planned to get supplies before flooding returned.

 Freshman Noah Julian was among those caught in the earlier flooding. He stepped off his school bus to find his neighborhood along Coleman Avenue flooded. A video recorded by neighbor Martina Elieson spread quickly on social media, showing him swimming through floodwaters to reach his driveway. His father, Romeo Julian, expressed concern about alligators, snakes and sharp objects in the water.

 Residents are encouraged to monitor local forecasts and prepare for changing conditions as the rain moves into the area.
